title: Ranil’s 10-point plan for Sri Lanka to survive new world order | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 06:26
-     - 514

Former President  Ranil Wickremesinghe

FORMER President Ranil Wickremesinghe has set out a 10-point plan for Sri Lanka to secure a place in an emerging world order, with rapid technological modernisation, membership of BRICS, and a stronger maritime role at its core.

“If we do not do this, we will have no place in the new world order,” Wickremesinghe said, delivering the keynote at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with Women in Management (WIM), the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo, and Pioneer Institute of Business and Technology, on Saturday. The webinar was titled “In an Emerging New World Order, What Are Sri Lanka’s Options?”

Among the requirements he set out were rapid technological modernisation resulting in a strong, competitive economy, making Sri Lanka a maritime logistics centre, close economic cooperation with India, and stronger relations with Bay of Bengal and other Southeast Asian countries, leading finally to regional integration. He also urged Sri Lanka to join BRICS, strengthen relations with the US, China, and Russia, as well as Japan, engage in transactional geopolitics, accelerate the work of the Colombo Security Conclave, and build a technologically advanced Navy with small and medium naval ships.

“If you want to survive in this new global order, where technology plays this role and trade will certainly have an importance, either we have to go along this way or fade into insignificance like one of the small Pacific Isles,” he said.

Wickremesinghe framed his proposals around Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s address at the NDTV World Summit, which characterised the present as a world between orders, with one ending and another beginning. Modi had highlighted the weaponising of finance, trade, technology, and shipping as part of the new geopolitics, he noted, adding that post-World War II institutions were unable to intervene as they had not adapted to the changing order. Modi had also invoked Chanakya on the need to prevent Matsya Nyaya, where the strong swallow the weak.

Citing a Goldman Sachs report, Wickremesinghe said Artificial Intelligence (AI) and data ownership, combined with dollar-dominated global financial markets, formed the basis of US dominance, while China, the other AI superpower, was seeking an alternative with BRICS members. “What we are witnessing today is a duopoly of AI and computing superpowers,” he said, adding that China and the US also led in space, ocean, and automation technologies, while India, the UK, France, Germany, Israel, Japan, and South Korea were developing their own. “We have to remember sovereignty today implies technology.”

He said the decline of Western-led alliances was giving way to transactional geopolitics between the leading powers, and that Sri Lanka needed economic and social transformation based on technology-oriented modernisation, or it would be swallowed up.

The Indian Ocean, he said, would be one of the centres of the new order alongside the emerging economies of Asia and Africa, strengthening its role as the main shipping artery between East and West, with immense undersea resources available for exploration. However, the US-Iran war had eroded the Indian Ocean’s status as a zone of peace and its freedom of navigation, he said, making it Sri Lanka’s interest to ensure that its two economic lifelines, the Suez Canal and the Gulf, remained fully operational.

He urged policymakers not to ignore the Bay of Bengal as an economic region. Indonesia, projected to have the fourth or fifth largest GDP by 2050, would extend its influence, and Bangladesh would also emerge as an economic power, he said. Closer economic cooperation between Southeast Asia and Western China was producing the Chengdu-Chongqing corridor extending to Myanmar and Bangladesh, which he said would give China a second access to the Indian Ocean, this time through the Bay of Bengal. He also pointed to an economic region at Sri Lanka’s doorstep, a market of 600 million excluding India.

Emerging technologies, including orbital maritime awareness satellites, hypersonic weapons, unmanned water vehicles, and drones, would play a major role in Indian Ocean security, he said, adding that protecting undersea cables in the region was a priority.

On trade, Wickremesinghe, who said he had worked on agreements with Singapore and Thailand, named Indonesia, Malaysia, and Vietnam as the next targets. While Europe and the US remained important markets, Sri Lanka could not send more goods there and had to find markets elsewhere in Asia, “because that’s where the power is going to be.”

“We are a hundred billion dollar GDP. We are so small. Most American corporations are bigger than that. So is Tata or Adani. We have to realise that and we must grow big,” he said.

On the US midterm elections, he said foreign policy was unlikely to play a big role, and that both Vice President JD Vance and the Democrats appeared inclined to withdraw from global affairs, with the US relying instead on its financial and technological power. How the big powers and India drew their relations would determine “where and how we can play our pieces on the chessboard,” he said. “But to play the pieces on the chessboard, we have to become a strong economy. Otherwise, you are nowhere.”

On AI, he warned of the emergence of trillion-dollar companies on both the US and Chinese sides, its impact on employment in India and Sri Lanka, and rising social tensions in the UK, France, and Germany if wealth concentrated among a handful of trillionaires. “We must know how to harness AI,” he said.

title: British Airways celebrates return to Sri Lanka with special fares | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 06:39
-     - 232

British Airways Captain Terry Smith and Hayleys Chairman and Chief Executive Mohan Pandithage cut a cake to celebrate the resumption of direct services on Saturday. British High Commissioner Andrew Patrick, British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright, Civil Aviation Authority Director General and CEO Capt. Daminda Rambukwella, British Airways Senior First Officer Pradeeb Vimalraj, IAG Cargo Regional Commercial Manager – Asia Pacific, India and Middle East Ankush Chawla and Hayleys Advantis Managing Director Ruwan Waidyaratne are among those who look on

British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright

The crew of the first British Airways flight

By Nisthar Cassim

British Airways on Saturday marked a significant milestone with the arrival of its first flight into Colombo, reconnecting Sri Lanka with the UK for the first time in over 11 years.

The inaugural flight, operated by Sri Lankan crew, was welcomed by traditional dancers and drummers on arrival to commemorate the occasion. The new route strengthens links between the two countries, supporting tourism, trade, and business travel. 

The thrice-weekly service will be operated by British Airways’ Boeing 777 fleet, featuring Club World (business class), World Traveller Plus (premium economy), and World Traveller (economy) cabins.

To celebrate the launch, British Airways is offering special return fares with savings of up to 10% in World Traveller, starting from Rs. 255,000 for travel from Colombo to London Gatwick.

British Airways Chief Planning and Strategy Officer Neil Chernoff in a statement said the resumption marks a special moment for British Airways, as it meant bringing Sri Lanka back to its global network and giving customers greater choice when planning their next getaway.

“Sri Lanka is renowned for its warmth, rich culture, and hospitality, and we’re delighted to be flying there once again. To celebrate, we’re offering special fares and look forward to welcoming customers on board,” he added.

Noting that Sri Lanka is one of the first re-entries in recent months, British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright during a media interaction post-first flight on Saturday stressed that Sri Lanka has always been a really important market for British Airways.

“Between the UK and Sri Lanka, we have deep cultural and historic links, and so it is a market that we continue to keep an eye on. And obviously, over the last few years, we have seen that economic growth and tourism rebound post-COVID, and we continue to review our network, and we felt that the time was right to reintroduce our services from this winter,” he told journalists in Colombo.

Wright said that a heart of a business case like this is very much tourism from the UK coming into the incredible island of Sri Lanka and everything it has to offer. “But we have also seen really positive demand across sectors: tourism going into the UK, but also across business sectors and also people visiting communities and friends and family as well.”

He described the all-inclusive offers starting from Rs. 255,000 as “compelling.” The Boeing 777 has a capacity of over 300 seats and Wright noted that British Airways has been really pleased with the response. The special fares in World Traveller (economy) on return flights from Colombo to Gatwick, available for booking until 15 November 2026, for outbound travel between 20 October and 30 November 2026 and inbound travel between 26 October and 10 December 2026.

British Airways General Sales Agents (GSA) Hayleys Advantis Ltd., Managing Director Ruwan Waidyaratne said: “The commencement of British Airways’ flight operations to Colombo marks a significant milestone in enhancing air connectivity between Sri Lanka and the UK. The service will offer customers greater travel options while supporting tourism and business travel between the two markets, and we look forward to continuing our partnership with British Airways.”

He said Hayleys’ relationship with British Airways dates back to 1995, and it is delighted to welcome the airline back to Sri Lanka as this longstanding partnership enters a new chapter.

Waidyaratne stressed that improved connectivity between Sri Lanka and the UK creates opportunities that extends beyond travel, supporting tourism, stimulating economic activities, and strengthening ties between the two countries.

“We look forward to seeing this connection grow and deliver lasting value for travellers, the tourism industry, and Sri Lanka as a whole,” he added.

Senior First Officer Pradeeb Vimalraj, who operated the airline’s inaugural flight in a statement said: “As a Sri Lankan, born and raised in Jaffna in my early years, bringing our first flight back home after more than a decade was particularly special. The warm welcome we received made it even more memorable, and I am so proud to be part of this new chapter connecting Sri Lanka and the UK.”

British Airways also revealed that searches on ba.com for flights from London to Colombo have increased by more than 10% in the past week, reflecting continued interest in the destination.

British Airways operates one of the largest and the most modern fleets of any airline in the world and is transforming the operations with a £ 7 billion investment plan.

Departure from Gatwick is at 1640 hours on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays and arrival in Colombo at 0935 hours the next day. Departure from Colombo is 1035 hours Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays with arrival at Gatwick at 1700 hours.

British Airways said the new service gives customers travelling from the UK direct access to one of South Asia’s most captivating destinations. From golden beaches and ancient cultural sites to wildlife reserves, tea country and a thriving food scene, Sri Lanka offers a diverse range of experiences for travellers to discover.

title: Digital deal can jump-start stalled ETCA: Wijesinha | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 06:34
-     - 91

CSF Co-Founder and Economist Anushka Wijesinha

Sri Lanka can revive stalled negotiations on the Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) with India by first concluding a standalone Digital Economy Agreement that builds on the momentum of recent bilateral digital cooperation, Centre for a Smart Future (CSF) Co-Founder and Economist Anushka Wijesinha said.

Wijesinha noted that the ETCA negotiations had dragged through 14 rounds over many years and multiple governments, with momentum slowing significantly on the Sri Lankan side. The present Government is awaiting the completion of a unilateral review of existing free trade agreements (FTAs) before deciding how to proceed with any new ones, while the ETCA and its predecessor, Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), carry political baggage as initiatives inherited from previous administrations.

Against this backdrop, he said digital connectivity had been driving a new phase in bilateral relations. Initiatives around digital payments integration led by India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), collaboration on digital public infrastructure, especially the digital ID project, and the emergence of trade settlement in Indian and Sri Lankan rupees have characterised this phase, building on India’s 2022 crisis-era assistance and relief following Cyclone Ditwah.

“Carving some of these initiatives out into an immediate, standalone Digital Economy Agreement can capture this momentum,” Wijesinha said.

He argued that converting ad hoc, episodic initiatives into mutually negotiated commitments, with defined obligations and review mechanisms, would place digital cooperation within a firm institutional framework. “An achievable ‘early harvest’ win here would inject fresh enthusiasm into Indo-Lanka economic integration, while demonstrating tangible benefits to domestic stakeholders,” he said.

Wijesinha pointed out that such a modular approach would not be unprecedented. India has already decided to unbundle investment chapters from comprehensive FTAs, expecting partners instead to sign Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) based on its Model BIT. This has been conveyed to Sri Lanka, and a new standalone BIT is expected to be signed rather than an investment chapter being included in the ETCA, as the Sri Lankan side had previously assumed.

Applying the same precedent to the digital sphere, he said, would allow both nations to advance high-value integration without getting bogged down by traditional trade bottlenecks.

For design, he suggested the two countries look to ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), recently concluded and now awaiting ratification by Member States. The DEFA grew out of each member economy’s post-COVID push towards digitalisation, expanding into a pan-regional ambition from 2023.

While acknowledging that sceptics might dismiss a 10-nation regional treaty as irrelevant to a bilateral relationship, Wijesinha said DEFA’s core value lay in how it navigated differences in scale and readiness among its members. Instead of demanding full regulatory harmonisation, which often triggers concerns over sovereignty and dominance, the framework relied on interoperability, tiering, sequencing, and flexible commitments.

“Rather than requiring Sri Lanka to harmonise its laws and systems to Indian standards, a DEFA-inspired interoperability approach would allow divergent national systems to recognise and transact with each other without enforcing identical rules,” he said, adding that this could be backed by tiered and possibly sequenced commitments, with periodic reviews allowing ambition to grow over time.

DEFA covers nine areas, ranging from payments and digital ID to cybersecurity, data flows, competition policy and talent mobility. However, Wijesinha said an India-Sri Lanka agreement need not cover all of these at once, and should focus on practical, non-controversial areas where collaboration is already underway or imminent. These include payment system interoperability, digital trade and paperless customs, treatment of cross-border e-commerce and digital goods, mutual legal recognition of e-signatures, cybersecurity cooperation, and cooperation on emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI).

Sensitive areas that risk stalling negotiations could be excluded, he said. Talent mobility is politically sensitive in Sri Lanka, and DEFA’s provisions on the preferential movement of digital talent and entrepreneurs are possible in ASEAN partly because labour mobility is less politically charged among its members. In Sri Lanka, liberalising Mode 4 services, which covers professionals temporarily crossing borders to deliver services, attracts considerable domestic sensitivity, as earlier CEPA and ETCA rounds showed.

Cross-border data flows are similarly difficult to model directly on DEFA’s default of free flow, he noted. India’s data protection regime leans towards retaining the ability to impose sector-specific data localisation requirements, while Sri Lanka is only just advancing its own data protection regime.

Wijesinha stressed that negotiating a digital agreement first did not mean abandoning the broader ambition for a comprehensive deal such as the ETCA, but could instead serve as a stimulant to the stalled process. He recalled that when the CEPA was envisioned, the Joint Study Group showed bold ambition by mapping extensive cooperation areas beyond goods trade, just three years after the first bilateral agreement came into force.

While such ambition and foresight appear to have dipped since, he said decoupling the digital agenda and forging a dedicated agreement could rekindle that forward-looking spirit, bring in new stakeholders and reflect contemporary aspirations on both sides.

“India and Sri Lanka must not let legacy trade hurdles hurt optimism for new areas of economic integration,” Wijesinha said.

He made these observations in an article for the Observer Research Foundation (https://www.orfonline.org/expert-speak/can-a-digital-economy-agreement-refresh-india-sri-lanka-economic-integration).

title: Finalise ETCA with India before other trade deals: Ranil | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 06:30
-     - 59

EX- President Ranil Wickremesinghe has called for Sri Lanka to finalise the Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) with India as its first trade priority, ahead of free trade agreements (FTAs) with other Asian economies.

“Our first one is that we have to do the agreement with India,” Wickremesinghe said, noting that the agreement was currently suspended. He was speaking at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with Women in Management (WIM), the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo, and Pioneer Institute of Business and Technology, on Saturday.

Asked whether India would change the global order, Wickremesinghe said that while the order currently appeared to rest on the US, China, and Russia, India could not be ignored. “It’s going to be the third-largest GDP in the world. It’s a military power and it is the dominant power in the Indian Ocean. So at some stage, India has to come in,” he said. The US, he noted, had also improved relations with Pakistan, and how it balanced these relationships would matter.

On managing relations with India and China, he said Sri Lanka and India were close and should be closer, keeping the spirit of the exchange of letters between Rajiv Gandhi and J.R. Jayewardene that neither country would do anything to harm the security of the other. Relations had evolved since the time of Emperor Ashoka according to developments in the world, he said.

“Now, it’s not a question of India or China, it’s how India and China manage their relationships,” he said. With China set to enter the Bay of Bengal, Myanmar and Bangladesh would become places of competing influence, he added, noting that India was strengthening its friendship with Myanmar and that both India and China, as BRICS members, would have to reach an understanding on how the region developed.

title: Experts outline Sri Lanka’s priorities in new world order | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 06:30
-     - 115

Sri Lanka must diversify its markets, build trusted digital trade institutions, and balance between competing powers while keeping its ties with the US strong if it is to turn its post-crisis recovery into lasting prosperity in a fragmenting world order, three international experts said.

International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Global Honorary Chair Maria Fernanda Garza, Switzerland-based political consultant, campaign strategist, and political scientist Dr. Louis Perron, and former Sri Lankan Ambassador to the US, Mexico and Trinidad and Tobago Mahinda Samarasinghe were speaking at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with Women in Management (WIM), the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo, and Pioneer Institute of Business and Technology, on Saturday. The webinar was titled “In an Emerging New World Order, What Are Sri Lanka’s Options?”

Garza, who visited Colombo in 2023 amid the economic crisis, said stability had since improved, growth had returned, and reforms were underway, but the world had changed profoundly. “We are not witnessing the end of globalisation, we are witnessing its transformation,” she said.

She identified three opportunities. The first was diversification and regional integration, as over-dependence on a few markets, suppliers, or partners created vulnerability. Sri Lanka’s Indian Ocean location, its ties with India, and its connections across Asia, Europe, and the US allowed it to deepen its role in regional value chains, logistics, services, and higher-value exports. “The objective should not be to choose between competing economic powers, but to build diversified relationships that preserve economic opportunity and strategic flexibility,” she said.

The second was digital transformation underpinned by institutional trust. Welcoming progress towards paperless customs, Garza cautioned that technology could make procedures faster without making them better. “The countries that benefit most will not necessarily be those that adopt technology fastest, but those that develop the institutional capacity to use it effectively,” she said.

The third was renewing international cooperation, as predictable rules were essential infrastructure for smaller economies, the most exposed when cooperation gave way to power-based negotiations, she said.

Samarasinghe, Ambassador in Washington for five years, said the US remained the world’s largest economy and importer, which was why leaders scrambled to strike deals after the Donald Trump Administration’s reciprocal tariffs of April 2025. Some 45 countries had since signed agreements under what he termed a carrot and stick approach, with Washington pursuing geopolitical objectives through trade talks.

The sticks included surcharges on buyers of cheap Russian oil, since rolled back but liable to return, and a 40% surcharge on Vietnam over transshipment. The US also insisted on bilateral terms, full or near-full duty-free access for its exports, and US standards for its agricultural exports, he said.

The carrot was a locked-in tariff rate, such as 15%, 19%, or 20%, shielded from fresh probes including Section 301 investigations, plus zero rating for thousands of goods. In return, partners made large pledges: the EU a non-binding $ 600 billion in investment and $ 750 billion in oil, gas, and nuclear fuel purchases, Japan $ 550 billion, Taiwan $ 500 billion, South Korea $ 300 billion, and India $ 500 billion.

While tariff pressure had expedited alternatives such as the India-EU free trade agreement (FTA) after 17 years of talks, the US would remain the predominant economic force, he said. He urged Sri Lanka to keep exercising “smart options,” citing its role in Operation Prosperity Guardian in the Red Sea under President Ranil Wickremesinghe and the present Government’s handling of the Iranian ship issue, which the White House and the State Department praised for keeping the US informed while maintaining neutrality. “It is in Sri Lanka’s interest to have the best of relations with the US,” he said.

Dr. Perron said Donald Trump’s return marked the end of sole US dominance after the Cold War, giving way to competing superpowers. A likely Democrat House majority after the midterms would deepen gridlock, leaving the world’s largest economy able to pass a budget only under threat of a Government shutdown, he said.

Regional and medium powers such as Turkey, Brazil, Saudi Arabia, and Indonesia would grow more assertive amid shifting alliances. “You get a better deal from the superpowers if you do a balancing act as a country,” he said, adding that Wickremesinghe had done an outstanding job of this for Sri Lanka.

The new order would be unstable, with regional wars likely, forcing many countries to follow the Israeli and Polish model of heavy defence spending while international law, the UN, and the World Trade Organisation (WTO) were sidelined, Dr. Perron warned. Citing the diverging fortunes of Colombia and Venezuela, Poland and Ukraine, and South and North Korea, he said the difference lay in the choices of political leadership.

title: PM tells CNN IMF priorities align with Govt.’s own | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 06:30
-     - 129

Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya

Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya has told CNN that several of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) priorities align with the Government’s own objectives, underpinning its decision to continue Sri Lanka’s IMF program despite her party’s earlier opposition.

Dr. Amarasuriya said the Government had been able to discuss its concerns with the IMF, particularly on governance, corruption, and fiscal discipline.

“When we came into power, the IMF agreement was already signed and we started working with them, and we found them approachable,” she told CNN’s Richard Quest of ‘Quest Means Business.’

Maintaining economic stability was among the administration’s immediate priorities following the election, she said, adding that the country had made considerable progress since the 2022 crisis.

“We are doing remarkably well given what we’ve been through,” she said.

The Prime Minister attributed the improvement primarily to fiscal management, financial discipline, efforts to address corruption and waste, and governance reforms. Two years into the administration, she said, the situation was ‘looking not too bad.’

Acknowledging that her party had opposed the IMF program due to Sri Lanka’s previous experiences with the institution, she said the Government had no choice but to continue it.

We didn’t like it because we felt that our previous experiences with the IMF have not been great. This is not the first time we’ve entered an IMF program,” she said.

She also acknowledged that the Government had faced pressure to demonstrate its ability to govern, saying many people had been waiting for it to fail.

Dr. Amarasuriya also reaffirmed Sri Lanka’s commitment to geopolitical neutrality and non-alignment, saying conflicts such as the war in the Middle East ‘serve no one.’

Sri Lanka’s geographical position in the Indian Ocean made it important for the country to stay clear of geopolitical conflicts amid rising global tensions, she said. Avoiding entanglement in international power struggles was essential for its national interests and economic stability, she stressed, particularly as the country faces the impact of rising fuel prices and global energy costs.

Acknowledging that maintaining balanced relations with major powers, including China, India, and the US, had historically been a key challenge for Sri Lanka’s foreign policy, she said aligning too closely with any single power had not worked to the country’s advantage. This, she said, underscored the importance of maintaining an independent foreign policy amid growing international tensions.

title: Sampath Bank’s  Rs. 10 b debenture issue oversubscribed by 22.7% | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 06:29
-     - 100

Sampath Bank PLC’s debenture issue was oversubscribed and closed at its maximum of Rs. 10 billion, having drawn applications worth Rs. 12.27 billion, with a small number of large-value payments made through Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) transfers and Letters of Guarantee accounting for nearly the entire amount.

According to the Registrars to the issue, Central Depository Systems Ltd., the bank received 31 applications for 122.66 million debentures as at 22 October, against a maximum of 100 million debentures on offer, oversubscribing the issue by 22.7%. Excess demand amounted to Rs. 2.27 billion, or 22.66 million debentures.

The issue comprised up to 100 million Basel III-compliant Tier 2 listed, rated, unsecured, subordinated, redeemable debentures with five-year (2026/2031) and seven-year (2026/2033) tenures, at a par value of Rs. 100 each. It was structured as an initial 70 million debentures to raise Rs. 7 billion, with an option to issue a further 30 million to raise Rs. 3 billion at the bank’s discretion in the event of an oversubscription.

Tier 2 debentures count towards a bank’s regulatory capital. Their non-viability conversion feature allows them to be converted into ordinary shares if the bank is deemed non-viable, meaning holders absorb losses ahead of depositors.

RTGS transfers, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL)-operated system for large-value interbank payments, were the dominant mode of payment. Eight applications paid via RTGS accounted for 80.5 million debentures worth Rs. 8.05 billion, or 65.6% of the total, an average of just over Rs. 1 billion per application.

Payments by Letter of Guarantee came to Rs. 3.5 billion for 35 million debentures from three applications, or 28.5% of the total.

In contrast, payments by bank drafts and cheques, which drew the highest number of applications at 20, amounted to Rs. 715.5 million for 7.16 million debentures, or 5.8% of the total value.

By type, Type A debentures attracted 25 applications for 99.01 million debentures worth Rs. 9.9 billion. Of this, RTGS transfers accounted for Rs. 5.95 billion from six applications, Letters of Guarantee for Rs. 3.25 billion from two applications, and bank drafts and cheques for Rs. 700.5 million from 17 applications.

Type B debentures drew six applications for 23.65 million debentures worth Rs. 2.37 billion. RTGS transfers accounted for Rs. 2.1 billion from two applications, a Letter of Guarantee for Rs. 250 million from one application, and bank drafts and cheques for Rs. 15 million from three applications.

title: Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturers gain global exposure at CPHI Worldwide 2026 in Milan | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 07:03
-     - 94

The Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), in collaboration with the Embassy of Sri Lanka in Rome and the Consulate General of Sri Lanka in Milan, facilitated an exposure visit for Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturers to the 37th edition of CPHI Worldwide 2026, held from 6 to 8 October 2026 at Fiera Milano, Milan, Italy. 

The program also included dedicated business networking sessions in Milan for the pharmaceutical sector.

A five-member business delegation representing five Sri Lankan companies participated in the exposure visit to explore opportunities to strengthen the international market presence of Sri Lankan manufacturers.

The participating companies were State Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Corporation, Siddhalepa Exports Ltd., Lina Manufacturing Ltd., Vetpharma Biotechnology Ltd., and Aithra Pharmaceuticals Ltd,, representing the pharmaceutical, veterinary, cosmeceutical and natural products sectors. The program provided an opportunity to gain exposure to international markets, explore potential business partnerships and identify avenues for expanding Sri Lanka’s presence in global markets.

CPHI Worldwide is a major international platform connecting stakeholders across the pharmaceutical value chain, including pharmaceutical manufacturers, active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) suppliers, contract development and manufacturing organisations (CDMOs), packaging providers, and specialist technical service companies. The event provides opportunities to explore emerging market trends, establish business relationships, and identify potential areas for commercial and technical cooperation.

Participation in the event enabled the Sri Lankan delegation to gain exposure to international pharmaceutical industry developments, explore potential export markets, and identify opportunities for collaboration with international industry stakeholders.

The pharmaceutical industry operates within a highly regulated environment, with manufacturers required to meet applicable product registration, quality, and regulatory requirements in both domestic and export markets. Obtaining market authorisation can be a lengthy and costly process, particularly in highly regulated markets where stringent manufacturing standards, including European Union Good Manufacturing Practice (EU-GMP) requirements, may apply.

Despite these developments, the sector continues to face challenges in keeping pace with evolving international market requirements, emerging products and technologies, regulatory frameworks, marketing strategies, new molecules, advanced manufacturing systems, and global pharmaceutical supply chains. Addressing these knowledge gaps is important to support the transition towards higher-value production and improved access to more regulated export markets.

Recognising these needs, the EDB facilitated the exposure visit to provide participating companies with opportunities to observe international industry developments, improve their understanding of global market expectations, and identify potential business and technology partnerships.

In addition to the exhibition visit, the Consulate General of Sri Lanka in Milan organised business networking sessions for the Sri Lankan delegation. These sessions provided participants with opportunities to engage with potential buyers, distributors, and other pharmaceutical industry stakeholders, explore prospective export markets, and discuss possible business collaborations.

The exposure visit to CPHI Worldwide 2026 enabled the Sri Lankan delegation to engage with international pharmaceutical companies and specialised service providers, including Barbados Pharmaceutical Inc. (Barbados), Orion GXP Consulting (Ireland), Gruppo Farmalpresa (Italy), Intertek (United Kingdom), Nanopharm (France) and NATAC (Spain), as well as representatives of the Ministry of Health of Tanzania. These engagements provided opportunities to explore potential business partnerships, technical cooperation, pharmaceutical product development, natural ingredients, regulatory requirements and international market development.

The EDB said it will continue to work with industry stakeholders and Sri Lanka’s overseas missions to promote Sri Lankan pharmaceutical products, facilitate international business linkages, and support the long-term development and competitiveness of the country’s pharmaceutical export sector.

title: Lankan envoy in Bangladesh meets Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 07:01
-     - 62

The High Commissioner of Sri Lanka to Bangladesh, Dharmapala Weerakkody, met with the Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DCCI) President Taskeen Ahmed, on 18 October 2026 at the DCCI office in Gulshan, Dhaka, to explore avenues for strengthening economic, trade and investment cooperation between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

The DCCI is a prominent private-sector business organisation in Bangladesh that represents businesses and entrepreneurs, particularly in Dhaka, and promotes trade, investment and industrial development through policy advocacy, business networking and public-private sector collaboration.

The discussions focused on enhancing bilateral trade and investment by creating opportunities for the business communities of both countries in pharmaceuticals, Information Technology (IT), renewable energy, logistics, tourism and other emerging sectors.

During the meeting, High Commissioner Weerakkody briefed the DCCI President on Sri Lanka Expo 2027, Sri Lanka’s premier international trade exhibition, scheduled to be held from 14 to 17 January 2027 at the Bandaranaike Memorial International Conference Hall (BMICH) in Colombo. He invited the DCCI to facilitate the participation of a business delegation at the exhibition, which will provide a platform for businesses from both countries to explore trade, investment and commercial partnerships.

The DCCI President welcomed the initiative and expressed a positive response to the proposed participation of a business delegation at Sri Lanka Expo 2027, highlighting the potential to strengthen business-to-business linkages and expand bilateral trade and investment.

Highlighting advances in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector in both countries, the DCCI President invited Sri Lanka to participate in the “Bangladesh AI Business Summit 2026”, organised by the DCCI in partnership with the Ministry of Science and Technology (MoST) of Bangladesh. The Summit is scheduled to be held on 5 November 2026 at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Center (BCFCC) in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka.

The meeting also underscored the importance of strengthening direct engagement between the private sectors of Sri Lanka and Bangladesh and identifying new areas of collaboration to support sustained economic growth and closer bilateral relations.

title: National forum to strengthen dialogue in public service | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 05:47
-     - 18

Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry Secretary S. Alokabandara (left) hands over the Declaration on Social Dialogue in the Public Service to Secretary to the President Dr. Nandika Sanath Kumanayake at the launch of the National Public Service Forum

The Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry in partnership with the International Labour Organisation (ILO), last week launched the National Public Service Dialogue Forum.

The Forum provides a formal and structured space for government administrators and public service employees across the country to discuss workplace issues and concerns. It allows workplace challenges and grievances to be addressed through dialogue and joint problem-solving. By improving workplace relations and strengthening accountability, the Forum aims to contribute to a public service that is more responsive and resilient.

The framework operates at three levels—workplace, sectoral and national—so that issues can be addressed at the appropriate level. Workplace forums deal with issues within individual institutions. Issues that cannot be resolved there can be taken to sectoral forums. The National forum addresses issues that affect more than one sector or require action by central government authorities.

Public Service handed over by Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry Secretary S. Alokabandara said: “The National Public Service Dialogue Forum gives administrators and employees a permanent space to raise concerns early and resolve them together, so that services to citizens continue without interruption. It can also help ensure that reforms, including digitalization and training, take account of the experience of the people responsible for delivering public services.”

Established workplace forums have already demonstrated how dialogue was used to address challenges ranging from promotion processes to workplace safety, while identifying ways to strengthen organizational performance and improve service delivery. Building on this experience, the national forum aims to contribute to peacebuilding, strengthen institutional resilience and social cohesion, and improve overall public service delivery.

United Nations Resident Coordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche said: “Public services are where people experience government in their everyday lives. Strengthening those services also means strengthening trust between people and institutions. This Forum is a recognition that lasting peace must be built through dialogue, inclusion and social justice, not enforcement alone.”

ILO Country Office for Sri Lanka and the Maldives Director Joni Simpson said:  “Social dialogue helps build trust between public institutions and workers by providing a structured way to raise concerns, discuss solutions and manage change. This is essential to preventing disputes and supporting a public service that responds effectively to people’s needs.”

The establishment of the National Forum is supported by the “Social Dialogue for Peace and Crisis Prevention in Sri Lanka” project, which promotes inclusive approaches to dispute resolution and strengthens cooperation across public institutions. This project is implemented by the International Labour Organisation (ILO), United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).

The launch of the National Forum reflects a shift towards more proactive, collaborative governance, recognising that meaningful worker participation, responsive institutions and constructive engagement between government and employees can contribute to lasting peace and economic stability.

title: Sri Lanka, Romania hold sixth round of political consultations | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 26 October 2026 05:46
-     - 29

The sixth round of Sri Lanka–Romania Political Consultations was successfully concluded on 22 October 2026 at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Romania, marking an important step in advancing bilateral relations.

Established under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed in 2013, the consultations serve as a platform for reviewing bilateral relations and exchanging views on regional and global developments.

The consultations were Co-chaired by the Sri Lankan Foreign Affairs and Foreign Employment Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra, and the Romanian State Secretary for Strategic Affairs Ana Cristina Tinca.

Reviewing the progress made since the fifth round of consultations held in Colombo in June 2023, Deputy Minister Hemachandra briefed the Romanian delegation on Sri Lanka’s progress towards economic stabilisation and macroeconomic resilience. He highlighted the governance reforms introduced since late 2024 following the election that gave the incumbent administration a two-thirds parliamentary majority, enabling the Government to address economic challenges and strengthen anti-corruption measures.

Reaffirming Sri Lanka’s longstanding foreign policy of neutrality and universal friendship, Hemachandra emphasised that strengthening strategic, trade and diplomatic ties with Romania remained an important priority for Sri Lanka.

State Secretary Tinca outlined Romania’s political landscape following the investiture of a new Government on 21 October 2026. She highlighted Romania’s strengths in high-value and high-growth sectors, including the chemical industry, green energy infrastructure and advanced cybersecurity, and invited further bilateral engagement in these areas.

Human capital and labour cooperation featured prominently in the discussions, with Deputy Minister Hemachandra, noting that Romania had been a preferred destination for Sri Lankan professionals since 2016.

Both delegations welcomed recent amendments to Romania’s foreign worker recruitment laws, which complemented the MoU on Labour Cooperation signed in March 2026. Emphasising the importance of safe, ethical and orderly labour mobility, the Co-Chairs acknowledged the untapped potential for commercial cooperation and agreed to expedite pending bilateral agreements and MoUs.

The Co-Chairs also exchanged views on evolving multilateral developments and agreed to expand cooperation in key sectors, including academic exchanges, education, tourism, import and export, and social protection.

Both delegations further agreed to strengthen institutional ties through Consular and Police cooperation to combat transnational organised crime. To mark the growing friendship between the two countries, both sides agreed to organise a series of commemorative events in 2027 to celebrate the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Sri Lanka and Romania.

Deputy Minister Hemachandra conveyed Sri Lanka’s interest in hosting the seventh round of Sri Lanka–Romania Political Consultations in Colombo in the latter part of 2027 to maintain the momentum of bilateral engagement.

The Sri Lankan delegation included the Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Romania Samantha Pathirana; the Director General for Europe and North America of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Dilani Weerakoon, and the Counsellor of the Embassy Prarthana Kaushalya.

The Romanian delegation included the Director Diana Tase, the Minister-Counsellor Albert Robu, the Second Secretary Theodora Drăgulescu, the Diplomatic Attaché of the Asia-Pacific and Latin America Division Vlad Popescu, and a representative of the National Visa Centre of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Romania Gabriela Ionescu.
